ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), a new class of environmentally friendly solvents, are gaining more attention from researchers for extracting and separating targeted analytes from different complex samples. DESs are liquid at room temperature and contain a hydrogen bond donor and a hydrogen bond acceptor. DESs are non-volatile solvents, have excellent thermal and electrical stability, and can easily dissolve a number of organic and inorganic substances. DESs have attracted a lot of attention as new green solvents are expected to take the place of traditional organic solvents. DESs are sustainable solvents that concern significant interest from researchers and various industries. They are non-flammable, chemically stable, biocompatible, biodegradable, and have low volatile content. DESs have tunable physicochemical properties that can be tailored to meet the needs of a definite task. This review summarizes the DESs-based adsorbent materials and its preparation characterizations and application by highlighting the unique properties such as extraction and separation applications. To summarize the DESs-based applications, this review reported up-to-date data related to this field. and also provide an easy and single path to cover the DESs-based materials and its adsorption applications. This review exploits new DESs and DESs-based materials that are diversifing into extraction and separation due to the development of DESs.

## 1. Introduction Development in deep eutectic solvents (DESs) represents a significant advancement in green chemistry. DESs are typically characterized as binary or ternary combinations of substances that can associate primarily through hydrogen bonds. DESs are widely used around the world due to their unique characteristics. The term DESs was coined by Abbott et al., in 2003 [1]. Due to their importance and exciting potential, these solvents have emerged as a dynamic, novel, and interesting "green chemistry" subfield. DESs are an advanced class of ionic liquids (ILs); their synthesis is as simple as just combining two or more substances made up of hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs). HBAs are quartet phosphonium, ammonium, and mineral salts. HBDs are alcohols, organic acids, amides, and sucrose. DESs are molten in nature and prepared from a eutectic mixture of two

## 2. Chemistry of DESs DESs are unique solvents with unusual characteristics; the terms have been used interchangeably in many publications. DESs are fabricated as a eutectic mixture by combining Lewis or Bronsted acid and a base containing a mixture of anions and cations species. Furthermore, a eutectic system is a chemical compound mixture that exhibits a single chemical composition that freezes at lower

temperatures. The eutectic fact is given by joining the eutectic composition and temperature; due to different solvent properties and the fact that some DES constituents are not ionic, the term DESS was coined to distinguish them from ILs. DESs drop the freezing point in the eutectic mixture, which can be as much as a few Celsius. To synthesize a eutectic mixture, two or more constituents are mixed at a specific temperature. HBAs and HBDs can form a complex with the combined quaternary ammonium salt halide ion to form DESs. The interaction between HBAs and HBDs components has the potential to link them together via hydrogen bond interactions. DESs are classified based on their physicochemical properties, particularly their melting point, which should be lower than the melting point of each distinct component. DESs typically have a large freezing point depression and are liquid at temperatures below 423 K, most of which are liquid between room temperature and 343 K. In 2007, Abbott defined DES as R1R2R3- R4N+ X¯:Y, where X is a halide ion (often Cl¯), and Y is a complexing agent composed of Cat+X [3]. According to the literature, interest in DESs is significantly growing, particularly in various chemical, electrochemical and separation applications. Different types of salts and HBDs, or complexing agents, have been reported for these applications. Because of its low cost, eco-friendliness, and non-hazardous properties, ChCl has been widely used as an organic salt in preparation of eutectic solvents, typically in conjunction with economical and non-toxic HBDs such as urea, glycerol, ethylene glycol, or carboxylic acids. Table 1 shows the various types of HBA and HBD commonly used to form DESs. These DESs combinations are appealing because they have comparable physicochemical properties to traditional imidazolium-based ILs and can thus replace them in many applications. Compared to conventional organic solvents, DESs are known as environmentally friendly and non-volatile organic solvents and non-flammable, making storage convenient.

### 3. Green chemistry scenario With the advent of green chemistry, using eco-friendly and non-hazardous solvents has become mandatory. The concept of "green" solvents indicates the desire to reduce the environmental effect caused by using solvents in manufacturing chemicals. Several solvents that might be utilized in the extraction process may be referred to as "green solvents" in light of this. Green solvents are non-volatile, non-toxic, recyclable, biodegradable, and cost-effective. Fig. 1 shows different solvents that meet this requirement. They are classified into four different types such as supercritical fluids, bio-based, supramolecular, and neoteric solvents. It is not simple to switch out a hazardous solvent for a more environmentally friendly substitute in a separation process; in some instances, new challenges and limitations can appear because of the different physicochemical characteristics of the solvents under consideration. Supercritical fluids (SCFs) are substances that have pressure and temperature values that are higher than their critical values. Gas-liquid characteristics, such as liquid density, solvating properties, gas-like viscosity, and diffusivity, define SCFs. As a result, they are ideal solvents for supercritical fluid extraction (SFC) operations. Solvents from renewable biomass sources, such as plant products, energy crops, waste materials, and aquatic biomass, are "bio-based solvents" prepared in the biorefinery, which seeks maximal extraction recovery and the creation of high-value products. Nanostructured liquids are known as supramolecular solvents (SUPRASS). SUPRASS are fabricated by the colloidal suspensions of amphiphiles through the spontaneous sequential mechanisms of self-assembly and coacervation. Fig. 1 shows the different types of green solvents.

## 4. Classification of DESs DESs were divided into four categories based on the general formula Cat + X zY, where Cat + indicates ammonium, phosphonium, or sulfonium and X is a Lewis base, typically a halide anion, in order to distinguish between the potential eutectics. The amount of Y molecules interacting with the associated anion is denoted by the symbol Y, which stands for a Lewis or Brnsted acid. Types of DESs such as I, II, III and IV. DESs comprise metal salts (hydrated metal chlorides) and other neutral compounds or organic salts. The most extensively researched eutectics are type III, which typically use choline chloride and a variety of hydrogen bond donors. Choline chloride has been widely used because it is reasonably inexpensive, non-toxic, and biodegradable. In actuality, choline chloride was the main component of the first type III deep eutectic solvent. Quaternary ammonium or phosphonium salts are the common hydrogen bond donors, while amides, alcohols, and carboxylic acids are the most typical hydrogen bond, acceptors. For manufacturing NADESS, substances including sugars, sugar alcohols, and amino acids are also considered. Hydrophobic DESs were introduced more recently. They work by using long alkyl chain alcohols and carboxylic acids as hydrogen bond donors, along with bromide, menthol, thymol, and fatty acids as hydrogen bond acceptors. Fig. 2 shows the classification of DESs. Additionally, active pharmacological components, including ibuprofen, lidocaine, and phenylacetic acid, can be used to prepare DESs. The solvents of hydrophobic substances, such as tetrabutylammonium, are then referred to as therapeutic DESs. On the other hand, it is occasionally possible to classify NADESs as type III deep eutectic solvents. A special type of DESs called NADESS was proposed during the development process described above. NADESS are made up of CHCl and natural components, such as water. In the NADESs system,

water helps to make the oil less thick. Choi et al. said the NADES system was made through the hydrogen bonding between the different parts. Most of the time, the HBAs comprise amines or amino acids, and the HBDs contain carbohydrates. So, the NADES are environmentally friendly and cheaper than other type III DESs. DESs are water-soluble because almost all of their parts have several hydroxyls, carboxyl, or amino groups [5].

5. Preparation of DESs DESs are synthesized using natural and renewable constituents and have analogous physicochemical characteristics to ILs. DESs are typically made up of bi- or tri-components of hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, such as acid amides and quaternary ammonium salts with lower melting points [6]. The easiest way to prepare DESs, which use all their atoms, is to mix HBAs and HBDs. The most common way to make DESs called the "heating and stirring method," is to mix and stir two or more components at a higher temperature (ordinarily 80 °C) until homogeneous liquid forms. This method was suggested by Abbott et al., in 2003. Different research groups use heating and stirring methods, and the reaction temperature (50–100 °C) is usually changed to fit the other reaction parts. Most DESs contain quaternary ammonium salt, which means that the DESs made by heating and stirring will have some water. Gutierrez et al. [7] came up with two other ways to make DESs using evaporating and freeze-drying processes) that don't involve water. Florindo et al. [8] also developed a way to make DESs that didn't affect high temperatures. When DESs (choline chloride: glutaric) is made by grinding, they are purer than when made by heating and stirring. The reaction between the carboxylic acid and the component with an OH group could also lead to the formation of esters.

## 6. Characterization DESs characterization is also an essential part of a study to check the formation of newly prepared DESs different techniques have been used, such as Proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR). 1H NMR spectroscopy can investigate hydrogen-bonding interactions and the formation of DES-specific halide ion hydrogen bond-donor supramolecular complexes. FTIR spectroscopy is a useful tool for determining hydrogen bonding and active functionality in DESs; a number of changes happened. In order to learn more information about the potential interactions, structural changes, and hydrogen bond formation in DESs, it is helpful to compare the FTIR spectrum of DESs with each of its constituent parts. The DESs' FTIR spectra showed several differences.

7. Physical and chemical properties of DESs The physical and chemical characteristics of DESs also influence the adsorption process. During the elimination procedure, volatile solvents are typically the most common media utilized, particularly for liquid and solid-liquid extraction. On the other hand, certain compounds degrade when exposed to volatile solvents, making the elimination and adsorption of target analytes very challenging. In addition, their quantitative analysis will invariably result in unforeseen errors. Methanol, dichloromethane, toluene, and acetonitrile are organic solvents with higher toxicity levels. These solvents have different affinities to water than other organic solvents. On the other hand, several extraction techniques have limitations, such as additional energy sources, heat, microwaves, or ultrasound, ultimately leading to the evaporation of organic solvents. 7.3. Density Density is also a fundamental physical property of DESs; density plays an important role in solvent design and selection in the extraction process. In general, the density of DESs depends on how their molecules are packed together and how strongly their parts interact. Most DESs have lower densities than water, and some have the same densities as water, which is better for the sample pre- treatment and preparation process. Ibrahim et al. [14] said that the density of DESs changes with temperature. At room tempera- ture, MTPB/EG had a density of 1.25 g/cm³, but at 80 °C, it had a density of 1.21 g/cm³. At 80 °C, the densities of the DESs of N4444eBr/EG and ChCl/EG were 1.03 g/cm³ and 1.09 g/cm³, respectively. Martins et al. found that as the length of the mono- carboxylic acid's alkyl chain increases, the density of DESs made of menthol and monocarboxylic acid decreases. In contrast to DESs made from menthol, DESs made from thymol get denser as the length of the alkyl chain in the monocarboxylic acid increases.

## 7.4. Surface tension DESs' surface tension is a crucial characteristic since it is closely related to the strength of the intermolecular interactions between the hydrogen bond donor and the associated salt. High surface tension is seen in highly viscous liquids, though. The values concerning the reported DESs typically range between 35 and 75 mN m1 at 25 °C. For sugar-based DESs such as choline chloride: D-glucose and choline chloride: D-fructose, again, exceptional high values were noted, reflecting their vast hydrogen-bond network. Additionally, the surface tension is influenced by the cation type and salt mole fraction since quaternary ammonium salts with more hydroxyl groups or longer alkyl chains have greater surface tensions. As the temperature rises, the surface tension also linearly decreases. Surface tension is affected by the strength of intermolecular interactions in DESs and temperature. The surface tension of most DESs is higher than that of conventional solvents. In extraction techniques, DESs with a low surface tension could be applied as a wetting or adhesive agent.

7.5. Polarity and solubilizing properties The polarity of a DESs is essential for its miscibility in the sample solution or other solvents and its solubilizing proficiency toward the targeted analytes. DESs are well known for dissolving polar and

weak-polar compounds such as drugs, pharmaceutical ingredients, metal oxides, carbon dioxide, and elemental species such as lead, mercury, and cadmium. Furthermore, DESs demonstrated a better solubilizing effect and thus better extractability when compared to conventional solvents. These characteristics can be reorganized moderately by the "like dissolves like" theory, which aids in selecting the appropriate DESs in terms of polarity. DESs have recently been tailored to specific by selecting distinct components based on the analytes using silico procedures. The novel interactions of DESs with target analytes allow for the selective separation of traces of this analyte from complex matrices. It should be noted that increasing the temperature generally decreases the polarity of DESs due to a decrease in the solvent's hydrogen-bond donating acidity, as observed with choline chloride/glycerol DESs [15].

7.6. pH The pH of the DESs can affect the charge of the bioactive com-pounds during the elimination process and thus the adsorption efficiency. Analytes are generally much easier to extract in their neutral forms using weakly polar solvents. As a result, the extrac-tion procedure pH should be higher than or close to the pKa values of the analytes being studied. The pH of various DESs varies with temperature, and the type of hydrogen bond donor heavily in-fluences their acidity. Because highly polar molecules require an acidic environment for extraction, organic acid- DESs or some natural DESs are frequently the best choices. This was seen with organic acid-based natural DESs, which produced the best extrac-tion results for anthocyanin (polar compounds). In contrast, sugar-based natural DESs were better for other phenolic compounds. pH highly influences protein extraction because of its amphoteric properties, and their isoelectric point should be considered [16].

7.7. Hydrogen bond Hydrogen bonding is a unique form of dipole-dipole attraction between molecules. It results from the attractive force between hydrogen atoms covalently bound to a highly electronegative atom. Hydrogen bond plays a crucial role in the formation and stability of DESs. DESs have been produced utilizing a variety of hydrogen bond donors, including carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amides. These liquids are easy to make and relatively unreactive with water; many are biodegradable and inexpensive. DESs are exceptionally flexible because of the wide range of hydrogen bond donors available. The hydrogen bond donor determines the solvent's physical properties and can be easily modified for specific uses. ## 9. Conclusion Adsorption is essential in analytical procedures, mainly when the environmental sample analysis or sample matrices are complex. Analytical performance is significantly impacted by selecting the best adsorbent solvent. The DESs have a broad spectrum of applications in the separation sciences, not just for their "greenness" but also for their extraordinary physicochemical properties. The DESs-based adsorbent has excellent molecular recognition efficiency in the aqueous phase. It is prepared in the aqueous media, escaping the consumption of a large quantity of traditional organic solvents. Due to its outstanding property, it simultaneously plays a porogen and imprinting path for the targeted analyte. Because of its ionizable nature, in the DESs the stronger hydrogen bonding, offers unique behaviour from the traditional solvents when used in the extraction process. However, the DESs-based adsorbents applications are still deficient, and the advantages of DESs over the outdated solvents have not been fully revealed. So that more efforts should be made to examine better DESs species for chromatographic separation techniques. It will be stimulating to explore the DESs adsorbents-based new environmental applications.

## 10. Future aspects The DESs-based adsorbent materials need more attention and research to explore the new modifications and applications in the separation sciences. DESs-based adsorbent materials have been used successfully to extract and separate a wide range of analytes like aromatic hydrocarbons, biodiesel, gases, metal, and metal. Still, researchers focused on modifying mobile and stationary phases for chromatographic techniques such as GC and HPLC; additionally, DESs should be used for the sample preparation for chromatographic determination. So it can be predicted that the use of DESs should be enhanced to advance new robust and chromatographic methods. In this prospect, it must be explored the temperature
effect and the effect of water quantity on the DESs preparation and stability.

It is important to emphasize different applied fields such as electrochemistry, separation sciences, pharmaceuticals and drug delivery if we expect that DESs will be used in analytical chemistry in ways other than as extractants. The use of DESs in this field has enormous potential that is essentially unexplored. Only a little bit of work has been completed in this area. Additionally, more research needs to be done on how DESs affect chromatography separation, including the potential use of DESs as a stationary phase in gas chromatography, a capillary modifier, or a mobile phase in electrophoresis as substitutes for ionic liquids. A wide range of work is also made possible by synthesizing and modifying adsor-bents in DESs media for additional applications in analytical chemistry. The scope of study in this field virtually expands to in-finity when we consider that it is possible to combine several areas, such as the fabrication of MIPs on the surface of electrodes in a DES medium. Therefore, we suggest that analytical chemistry re-searchers concentrate on using the potential application of DESs in the separation sciences and employing them in various areas. In actuality, DESs have not yet been used in conjunction with such directions as microfluidic analysis, the creation of paper micro-chips, luminescence and chemiluminescence, surface plasmon resonance, electrophoresis, sampling, and sample preparation. In the future, combining nanotechnology with DESs needs deep exploration and applications in separation sciences. Combining nanotechnology and DESs will open new doors in the separation sciences.

DESs are liquid at room temperature and contain a hydrogen bond donor and a hydrogen bond acceptor. DESs are non-volatile solvents, have excellent thermal and electrical stability, and can easily dissolve a number of organic and inorganic substances. DESs have attracted a lot of attention as new green solvents are expected to take the place of traditional organic solvents. DESs are sustainable solvents that concern significant interest from researchers and various industries. They are non-flammable, chemically stable, biocompatible, biodegradable, and have low volatile content. DESs have tunable physicochemical properties that can be tailored to meet the needs of a definite task. This review summarizes the DESs-based adsorbent materials and its preparation characterizations and application by highlighting the unique properties such as extraction and separation applications. To summarize the DESs-based applications, this review reported up-to-date data related to this field. and also provide an easy and single path to cover the DESs-based materials and its adsorption applications. This review exploits new DESs and DESs-based materials that are diversifing into extraction and separation due to the development of DESs. © 2022 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. ## 1. Introduction Development in deep eutectic solvents (DESs) represents a significant advancement in green chemistry. DESs are typically characterized as binary or ternary combinations of substances that can associate primarily through hydrogen bonds. DESs are widely used around the world due to their unique characteristics. The term DESs was coined by Abbott et al., in 2003 [1]. Due to their importance and exciting potential, these solvents have emerged as a dynamic, novel, and interesting "green chemistry" subfield. DESs are an advanced class of ionic liquids (ILs); their synthesis is as simple as just combining two or more substances made up of hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs). HBAs are quartet phosphonium, ammonium, and mineral salts. HBDs are alcohols, organic acids, amides, and sucrose. DESs have some distinguishing characteristics, including simple and green synthetic processes, cost-effectiveness, environmentally friendly, with high efficiency, making them suitable for large-scale production. According to Abbott et al., the scheme and preparation of DESs are still in their early stages, and more research is required. DESs is a hot research era in different workplaces with novel and emerging applications, especially in chemistry, metals, bio- materials, separation sciences, electrochemistry, organocatalysis, solar technology, and photosynthesis. Since realizing the potential for viable chemical methodol-ogies, in the last decade, researchers have focused on DESs [2]. Some particular DESs types have also received much attention, such as natural-DESS (NADESS) were proposed by Choi et al., in 2011. The eutectic mixtures are designed by principal cellular components, including alcohols, sugar, carboxylic acid, and amino acids. They hypothesized that the NADESs might play an essential role in a wide range of cellular processes that explain the mechanism and phenomena that would otherwise be difficult to comprehend, like the bio-synthesis of nonpolar smaller and larger molecules. This recommends that lipids and water not only are solvents in bio-spheres but also explain the bioactive compounds with high solu-bilizing capacity. Because of the natural component, NADESs have a significant advantage over DESs because they fully represent green chemistry principles. Surprisingly, in recent years, there has been an exponential growth of publications focusing on using environ-mentally friendly solvents such as DESs and water, both of which follow the green chemistry principles. DESs have unique physico-chemical characteristics (e.g., thermal stability, negligible vapor pressure, low cost, non-flammable, and a stronger hydrogen bond network. Intriguingly, DESs have another feature: they play a vital role in nature's game. NADESs are prepared from the primary metabolites (e.g., amino acids, sugars, carboxylic acids, vitamins, and natural amino alcohols). NADESs may allow biological pro-cesses to occur in living organisms in the interim as the liquid state in addition to lipid and water, assisting the storage and conveyance of poorly water-soluble macro-molecules and protecting biological systems from cold and drought stresses. Simultaneously, water plays an essential role in preparing NADESs by altering the physi-cochemical characteristics of the corresponding supramolecular network. As a result, NADESS interactions with natural and bio-materials are altered (vide infra). Although a bit of water in hy-drated DESs would strengthen the hydrogen-bond network, researchers have reported that the DESs nanostructure retains up to 42 wt percent of water. At 51% water weight, the solution begins to behave almost like solutes in an aqueous solution. Despite the similarities between DESs and water, when tested individually in specific reactions, these "solvents" in nature sometimes offer complimentary performances on organic reactivity. The reasons are still unknown, and researchers have considered understanding molecular mechanisms of action a hotly debated topic. The aim is to provide the readers with an overview of the wide range of possible reactions and the potential benefits of using DESs in (bio) synthetic processes synergistically or singly. The interested readers are referred to the comprehensive reviews/monographies already available in the literature. This review assists the scientific com-munity in studying the DESs-based adsorbent material to eliminate toxic pollutants from the environmental samples. This review focus on the new development in the DESs-based adsorbent material, especially in the synthesis, characterization, and environmental applications. It benefits multidisciplinary researchers and offers new ideas in different fields, including analytical chemistry, envi-ronmental, pharmaceutical, and biological. ## 2. Chemistry of DESs DESs are unique solvents with unusual characteristics; the terms have been used interchangeably in many publications. DESs are fabricated as a eutectic mixture by combining Lewis or Bronsted acid and a base containing a mixture of anions and cations species. Furthermore, a eutectic system is a chemical compound mixture that exhibits a single chemical composition that freezes at lower temperatures. The eutectic fact is given by joining the eutectic composition and temperature; due to different solvent properties and the fact that some DES constituents are not ionic, the term DESS was coined to distinguish them from ILs. DESs drop the freezing point in the eutectic mixture, which can be as much as a few Celsius. To synthesize a eutectic mixture, two or more constituents are mixed at a specific temperature. HBAs and HBDs can form a complex with the combined quaternary ammonium salt halide ion to form DESs. The interaction between HBAs and HBDs components has the potential to link them together via hydrogen bond interactions. DESs are classified based on their physicochemical properties, particularly their melting point, which should be lower than the melting point of each distinct component. DESs typically have a large freezing point depression and are liquid at temperatures below 423 K, most of which are liquid between room temperature and 343 K. In 2007, Abbott defined DES as R1R2R3- R4N+ X¯:Y, where X is a halide ion (often Cl¯), and Y is a complexing agent composed of Cat+X [3]. According to the literature, interest in DESs is significantly growing, particularly in various chemical, electrochemical and separation applications. Different types of salts and HBDs, or complexing agents, have been reported for these applications. Because of its low cost, eco-friendliness, and non-hazardous properties, ChCl has been widely used as an organic salt in preparation of eutectic solvents, typically in conjunction with economical and non-toxic HBDs such as urea, glycerol, ethylene glycol, or carboxylic acids. These DESs combinations are appealing because they have comparable physicochemical properties to traditional imidazolium-based ILs and can thus replace them in many applications. Compared to conventional organic solvents, DESs are known as environmentally friendly and non-volatile organic solvents and non-flammable, making storage convenient. ### 3. Green chemistry scenario With the advent of green chemistry, using eco-friendly and non-hazardous solvents has become mandatory. The concept of "green" solvents indicates the desire to reduce the environmental effect caused by using solvents in manufacturing chemicals. Several solvents that might be utilized in the extraction process may be referred to as "green solvents" in light of this. Green solvents are non-volatile, non-toxic, recyclable, biodegradable, and cost-effective. Fig. 1 shows different solvents that meet this requirement. They are classified into four different types such as supercritical fluids, bio-based, supramolecular, and neoteric solvents. It is not simple to switch out a hazardous solvent for a more environmentally friendly substitute in a separation process; in some instances, new challenges and limitations can appear because of the different physicochemical characteristics of the solvents under consideration. Supercritical fluids (SCFs) are substances that have pressure and temperature values that are higher than their critical values. Gas-liquid characteristics, such as liquid density, solvating properties, gas-like viscosity, and diffusivity, define SCFs. As a result, they are ideal solvents for supercritical fluid extraction (SFC) operations. Solvents from renewable biomass sources, such as plant products, energy crops, waste materials, and aquatic biomass, are "bio-based solvents" prepared in the biorefinery, which seeks maximal extraction recovery and the creation of high-value products. Nanostructured liquids are known as supramolecular solvents (SUPRASS). In terms of new green extraction technologies, DESs have demonstrated significant promise, and in the years to come, it is anticipated that the industry will widely adopt them. DESs, an alternative to ILs, have similar properties to ILs but cost less to make since the raw ingredients are less expensive, less hazardous, and frequently biodegradable. Classification of DESs DESs were divided into four categories based on the general formula Cat + X zY, where Cat + indicates ammonium, phosphonium, or sulfonium and X is a Lewis base, typically a halide anion, in order to distinguish between the potential eutectics. The amount of Y molecules interacting with the associated anion is denoted by the symbol Y, which stands for a Lewis or Brnsted acid. Types of DESs such as I, II, III and IV. DESs comprise metal salts (hydrated metal chlorides) and other neutral compounds or organic salts. The most extensively researched eutectics are type III, which typically use choline chloride and a variety of hydrogen bond donors. Choline chloride has been widely used because it is reasonably inexpensive, non-toxic, and biodegradable. In actuality, choline chloride was the main component of the first type III deep eutectic solvent. Quaternary ammonium or phosphonium salts are the common hydrogen bond donors, while amides, alcohols, and carboxylic acids are the most typical hydrogen bond, acceptors. For manufacturing NADESS, substances including sugars, sugar alcohols, and amino acids are also considered. Hydrophobic DESs were introduced more recently. They work by using long alkyl chain alcohols and carboxylic acids as hydrogen bond donors, along with bromide, menthol, thymol, and fatty acids as hydrogen bond acceptors. Fig. 2 shows the classification of DESs. Additionally, active pharmacological components, including ibuprofen, lidocaine, and phenylacetic acid, can be used to prepare DESs. The solvents of hydrophobic substances, such as tetrabutylammonium, are then referred to as therapeutic DESs. On the other hand, it is occasionally possible to classify NADESs as type III deep eutectic solvents. A special type of DESs called NADESS was proposed during the development process described above. NADESS are made up of CHCl and natural components, such as water. In the NADESs system, water helps to make the oil less thick. Choi et al. said the NADES system was made through the hydrogen bonding between the different parts. Most of the time, the HBAs comprise amines or amino acids, and the HBDs contain carbohydrates. So, the NADES are environmentally friendly and cheaper than other type III DESs. DESs are water-soluble because almost all of their parts have several hydroxyls, carboxyl, or amino groups [5]. 5. Preparation of DESs DESs are synthesized using natural and renewable constituents and have analogous physicochemical characteristics to ILs. DESs are typically made up of bi- or tri-components of hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, such as acid amides and quaternary ammonium salts with lower melting points [6]. The easiest way to prepare DESs, which use all their atoms, is to mix HBAs and HBDs. The most common way to make DESs called the "heating and stirring method," is to mix and stir two or more components at a higher temperature (ordinarily 80 °C) until homogeneous liquid forms. This method was suggested by Abbott et al., in 2003. Different research groups use heating and stirring methods, and the reaction temperature (50–100 °C) is usually changed to fit the other reaction parts. Most DESs contain quaternary ammonium salt, which means that the DESs made by heating and stirring will have some water. Gutierrez et al. [7] came up with two other ways to make DESs using evaporating and freeze-drying processes) that don't involve water. Florindo et al. [8] also developed a way to make DESs that didn't affect high temperatures. When DESs (choline chloride: glutaric) is made by grinding, they are purer than when made by heating and stirring. The reaction between the carboxylic acid and the component with an OH group could also lead to the formation of esters. ## 6. The DESs' FTIR spectra showed several differences. 7. Physical and chemical properties of DESs The physical and chemical characteristics of DESs also influence the adsorption process. On the other hand, certain compounds degrade when exposed to volatile solvents, making the elimination and adsorption of target analytes very challenging. In addition, their quantitative analysis will invariably result in unforeseen errors. Methanol, dichloromethane, toluene, and acetonitrile are organic solvents with higher toxicity levels. Conclusion Adsorption is essential in analytical procedures, mainly when the environmental sample analysis or sample matrices are complex. Analytical performance is significantly impacted by selecting the best adsorbent solvent. The DESs have a broad spectrum of applications in the separation sciences, not just for their "greenness" but also for their extraordinary physicochemical properties. The DESs-based adsorbent has excellent molecular recognition efficiency in the aqueous phase. It is prepared in the aqueous media, escaping the consumption of a large quantity of traditional organic solvents. Due to its outstanding property, it simultaneously plays a porogen and imprinting path for the targeted analyte. Because of its ionizable nature, in the DESs the stronger hydrogen bonding, offers unique behaviour from the traditional solvents when used in the extraction process. However, the DESs-based adsorbents applications are still deficient, and the advantages of DESs over the outdated solvents have not been fully revealed. So that more efforts should be made to examine better DESs species for chromatographic separation techniques. It will be stimulating to explore the DESs adsorbents-based new environmental applications. ## 10. Future aspects The DESs-based adsorbent materials need more attention and research to explore the new modifications and applications in the separation sciences. DESs-based adsorbent materials have been used successfully to extract and separate a wide range of analytes like aromatic hydrocarbons, biodiesel, gases, metal, and metal. Still, researchers focused on modifying mobile and stationary phases for chromatographic techniques such as GC and HPLC; additionally, DESs should be used for the sample preparation for chromatographic determination. So it can be predicted that the use of DESs should be enhanced to advance new robust and chromatographic methods. In this prospect, it must be explored the temperature effect and the effect of water quantity on the DESs preparation and stability. It is important to emphasize different applied fields such as electrochemistry, separation sciences, pharmaceuticals and drug delivery if we expect that DESs will be used in analytical chemistry in ways other than as extractants. The use of DESs in this field has enormous potential that is essentially unexplored. Only a little bit of work has been completed in this area. Additionally, more research needs to be done on how DESs affect chromatography separation, including the potential use of DESs as a stationary phase in gas chromatography, a capillary modifier, or a mobile phase in electrophoresis as substitutes for ionic liquids. A wide range of work is also made possible by synthesizing and modifying adsor-bents in DESs media for additional applications in analytical chemistry. The scope of study in this field virtually expands to in-finity when we consider that it is possible to combine several areas, such as the fabrication of MIPs on the surface of electrodes in a DES medium. Therefore, we suggest that analytical chemistry re-searchers concentrate on using the potential application of DESs in the separation sciences and employing them in various areas. In actuality, DESs have not yet been used in conjunction with such directions as microfluidic analysis, the creation of paper micro-chips, luminescence and chemiluminescence, surface plasmon resonance, electrophoresis, sampling, and sample preparation. In the future, combining nanotechnology with DESs needs deep exploration and applications in separation sciences. Combining nanotechnology and DESs will open new doors in the separation sciences. Introduction Development in deep eutectic solvents (DESs) represents a significant advancement in green chemistry. DESs are typically characterized as binary or ternary combinations of substances that can associate primarily through hydrogen bonds. DESs are widely used around the world due to their unique characteristics. The term DESs was coined by Abbott et al., in 2003 [1]. Due to their importance and exciting potential, these solvents have emerged as a dynamic, novel, and interesting "green chemistry" subfield. DESs are an advanced class of ionic liquids (ILs); their synthesis is as simple as just combining two or more substances made up of hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs). HBAs are quartet phosphonium, ammonium, and mineral salts. HBDs are alcohols, organic acids, amides, and sucrose. The eutectic mixtures are designed by principal cellular components, including alcohols, sugar, carboxylic acid, and amino acids. They hypothesized that the NADESs might play an essential role in a wide range of cellular processes that explain the mechanism and phenomena that would otherwise be difficult to comprehend, like the bio-synthesis of nonpolar smaller and larger molecules. This recommends that lipids and water not only are solvents in bio-spheres but also explain the bioactive compounds with high solu-bilizing capacity. Because of the natural component, NADESs have a significant advantage over DESs because they fully represent green chemistry principles. Surprisingly, in recent years, there has been an exponential growth of publications focusing on using environ-mentally friendly solvents such as DESs and water, both of which follow the green chemistry principles. Intriguingly, DESs have another feature: they play a vital role in nature's game. NADESs are prepared from the primary metabolites (e.g., amino acids, sugars, carboxylic acids, vitamins, and natural amino alcohols). NADESs may allow biological pro-cesses to occur in living organisms in the interim as the liquid state in addition to lipid and water, assisting the storage and conveyance of poorly water-soluble macro-molecules and protecting biological systems from cold and drought stresses. Simultaneously, water plays an essential role in preparing NADESs by altering the physi-cochemical characteristics of the corresponding supramolecular network. As a result, NADESS interactions with natural and bio-materials are altered (vide infra). Although a bit of water in hy-drated DESs would strengthen the hydrogen-bond network, researchers have reported that the DESs nanostructure retains up to 42 wt percent of water. At 51% water weight, the solution begins to behave almost like solutes in an aqueous solution. Despite the similarities between DESs and water, when tested individually in specific reactions, these "solvents" in nature sometimes offer complimentary performances on organic reactivity. The reasons are still unknown, and researchers have considered understanding molecular mechanisms of action a hotly debated topic. The aim is to provide the readers with an overview of the wide range of possible reactions and the potential benefits of using DESs in (bio) synthetic processes synergistically or singly. The interested readers are referred to the comprehensive reviews/monographies already available in the literature. This review assists the scientific com-munity in studying the DESs-based adsorbent material to eliminate toxic pollutants from the environmental samples. This review focus on the new development in the DESs-based adsorbent material, especially in the synthesis, characterization, and environmental applications. It benefits multidisciplinary researchers and offers new ideas in different fields, including analytical chemistry, envi-ronmental, pharmaceutical, and biological. ## 2. Chemistry of DESs DESs are unique solvents with unusual characteristics; the terms have been used interchangeably in many publications. DESs are fabricated as a eutectic mixture by combining Lewis or Bronsted acid and a base containing a mixture of anions and cations species. Furthermore, a eutectic system is a chemical compound mixture that exhibits a single chemical composition that freezes at lower temperatures. The eutectic fact is given by joining the eutectic composition and temperature; due to different solvent properties and the fact that some DES constituents are not ionic, the term DESS was coined to distinguish them from ILs. DESs drop the freezing point in the eutectic mixture, which can be as much as a few Celsius. To synthesize a eutectic mixture, two or more constituents are mixed at a specific temperature. HBAs and HBDs can form a complex with the combined quaternary ammonium salt halide ion to form DESs. The interaction between HBAs and HBDs components has the potential to link them together via hydrogen bond interactions. DESs are classified based on their physicochemical properties, particularly their melting point, which should be lower than the melting point of each distinct component. DESs typically have a large freezing point depression and are liquid at temperatures below 423 K, most of which are liquid between room temperature and 343 K. In 2007, Abbott defined DES as R1R2R3- R4N+ X¯:Y, where X is a halide ion (often Cl¯), and Y is a complexing agent composed of Cat+X [3]. According to the literature, interest in DESs is significantly growing, particularly in various chemical, electrochemical and separation applications. Different types of salts and HBDs, or complexing agents, have been reported for these applications. Because of its low cost, eco-friendliness, and non-hazardous properties, ChCl has been widely used as an organic salt in preparation of eutectic solvents, typically in conjunction with economical and non-toxic HBDs such as urea, glycerol, ethylene glycol, or carboxylic acids. These DESs combinations are appealing because they have comparable physicochemical properties to traditional imidazolium-based ILs and can thus replace them in many applications. Compared to conventional organic solvents, DESs are known as environmentally friendly and non-volatile organic solvents and non-flammable, making storage convenient. ### 3. Green chemistry scenario With the advent of green chemistry, using eco-friendly and non-hazardous solvents has become mandatory. The concept of "green" solvents indicates the desire to reduce the environmental effect caused by using solvents in manufacturing chemicals. Several solvents that might be utilized in the extraction process may be referred to as "green solvents" in light of this. Green solvents are non-volatile, non-toxic, recyclable, biodegradable, and cost-effective. Fig. 1 shows different solvents that meet this requirement. They are classified into four different types such as supercritical fluids, bio-based, supramolecular, and neoteric solvents. It is not simple to switch out a hazardous solvent for a more environmentally friendly substitute in a separation process; in some instances, new challenges and limitations can appear because of the different physicochemical characteristics of the solvents under consideration. Supercritical fluids (SCFs) are substances that have pressure and temperature values that are higher than their critical values. Gas-liquid characteristics, such as liquid density, solvating properties, gas-like viscosity, and diffusivity, define SCFs. As a result, they are ideal solvents for supercritical fluid extraction (SFC) operations. Solvents from renewable biomass sources, such as plant products, energy crops, waste materials, and aquatic biomass, are "bio-based solvents" prepared in the biorefinery, which seeks maximal extraction recovery and the creation of high-value products. Nanostructured liquids are known as supramolecular solvents (SUPRASS). SUPRASS are fabricated by the colloidal suspensions of amphiphiles through the spontaneous sequential mechanisms of self-assembly and coacervation. Fig. 1 shows the different types of green solvents. Neoteric solvents have structurally unique or unusual physical and chemical properties that can be tailored for various applications by altering the chemical ingredients [50]. Fluorous solvents, ionic liquids, and eutectic solvents have attracted the most attention among neoteric solvents. DESs were developed to address the environmental problems associated with ILs. They are similar to ionic liquids in their physical and chemical properties but are easier to make, more stable, and cheaper. Most of them are also good for the environment. In terms of new green extraction technologies, DESs have demonstrated significant promise, and in the years to come, it is anticipated that the industry will widely adopt them. DESs, an alternative to ILs, have similar properties to ILs but cost less to make since the raw ingredients are less expensive, less hazardous, and frequently biodegradable. For several decades, DESs, particularly those comprised HBDs and HBAs species, have been regarded as green and environmentally friendly for certain characteristics. First, the intercalation of HBDs and HBAs species can generate liquids that are non-volatile, non-hazardous to the environment, and practical. In addition, the III and advanced types of DESs consist of metal chlorides and NADESs consisting of tertiary amines, carboxylic acids, and alcohols, which are frequently biodegradable and non-toxic, and their low reactivity with water makes them ideal solvents for a variety of analytical applications. In addition, their low production costs and wide availability of raw materials. Most DESs are solid at room temperature and have a high viscosity, which limits their use as extraction solvents. In addition to all of the benefits of DES, NADESS are even more environmentally favorable because they are derived from natural sources. Classification of DESs DESs were divided into four categories based on the general formula Cat + X zY, where Cat + indicates ammonium, phosphonium, or sulfonium and X is a Lewis base, typically a halide anion, in order to distinguish between the potential eutectics. The amount of Y molecules interacting with the associated anion is denoted by the symbol Y, which stands for a Lewis or Brnsted acid. Types of DESs such as I, II, III and IV. DESs comprise metal salts (hydrated metal chlorides) and other neutral compounds or organic salts. The most extensively researched eutectics are type III, which typically use choline chloride and a variety of hydrogen bond donors. Choline chloride has been widely used because it is reasonably inexpensive, non-toxic, and biodegradable. In actuality, choline chloride was the main component of the first type III deep eutectic solvent. Quaternary ammonium or phosphonium salts are the common hydrogen bond donors, while amides, alcohols, and carboxylic acids are the most typical hydrogen bond, acceptors. For manufacturing NADESS, substances including sugars, sugar alcohols, and amino acids are also considered. Hydrophobic DESs were introduced more recently. They work by using long alkyl chain alcohols and carboxylic acids as hydrogen bond donors, along with bromide, menthol, thymol, and fatty acids as hydrogen bond acceptors. Fig. 2 shows the classification of DESs. Additionally, active pharmacological components, including ibuprofen, lidocaine, and phenylacetic acid, can be used to prepare DESs. The solvents of hydrophobic substances, such as tetrabutylammonium, are then referred to as therapeutic DESs. On the other hand, it is occasionally possible to classify NADESs as type III deep eutectic solvents. A special type of DESs called NADESS was proposed during the development process described above. NADESS are made up of CHCl and natural components, such as water. In the NADESs system, water helps to make the oil less thick. Choi et al. said the NADES system was made through the hydrogen bonding between the different parts. Most of the time, the HBAs comprise amines or amino acids, and the HBDs contain carbohydrates. So, the NADES are environmentally friendly and cheaper than other type III DESs. DESs are water-soluble because almost all of their parts have several hydroxyls, carboxyl, or amino groups [5]. 5. Preparation of DESs DESs are synthesized using natural and renewable constituents and have analogous physicochemical characteristics to ILs. DESs are typically made up of bi- or tri-components of hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, such as acid amides and quaternary ammonium salts with lower melting points [6]. The easiest way to prepare DESs, which use all their atoms, is to mix HBAs and HBDs. The most common way to make DESs called the "heating and stirring method," is to mix and stir two or more components at a higher temperature (ordinarily 80 °C) until homogeneous liquid forms. This method was suggested by Abbott et al., in 2003. Different research groups use heating and stirring methods, and the reaction temperature (50–100 °C) is usually changed to fit the other reaction parts. Most DESs contain quaternary ammonium salt, which means that the DESs made by heating and stirring will have some water. Gutierrez et al. [7] came up with two other ways to make DESs using evaporating and freeze-drying processes) that don't involve water. Florindo et al. [8] also developed a way to make DESs that didn't affect high temperatures. When DESs (choline chloride: glutaric) is made by grinding, they are purer than when made by heating and stirring. The reaction between the carboxylic acid and the component with an OH group could also lead to the formation of esters. ## 6. Characterization DESs characterization is also an essential part of a study to check the formation of newly prepared DESs different techniques have been used, such as Proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR). 1H NMR spectroscopy can investigate hydrogen-bonding interactions and the formation of DES-specific halide ion hydrogen bond-donor supramolecular complexes. FTIR spectroscopy is a useful tool for determining hydrogen bonding and active functionality in DESs; a number of changes happened. In order to learn more information about the potential interactions, structural changes, and hydrogen bond formation in DESs, it is helpful to compare the FTIR spectrum of DESs with each of its constituent parts. The DESs' FTIR spectra showed several differences. 7. Physical and chemical properties of DESs The physical and chemical characteristics of DESs also influence the adsorption process. During the elimination procedure, volatile solvents are typically the most common media utilized, particularly for liquid and solid-liquid extraction. On the other hand, certain compounds degrade when exposed to volatile solvents, making the elimination and adsorption of target analytes very challenging. In addition, their quantitative analysis will invariably result in unforeseen errors. Methanol, dichloromethane, toluene, and acetonitrile are organic solvents with higher toxicity levels. These solvents have different affinities to water than other organic solvents. On the other hand, several extraction techniques have limitations, such as additional energy sources, heat, microwaves, or ultrasound, ultimately leading to the evaporation of organic solvents. The most important factors that influence the physicochemical properties of DESs are the combination structure of HBDs and HBAs. As a result, the following sections will study the available literature on the physicochemical characteristics of DESs and their applications. The properties of the DESs greatly influence the extraction efficiency. These properties are determined by the physicochemical properties of each DESs constituent and the in- teractions between the two components. The elimination efficiency is also influenced by the DESs solubilizing capacities and, eventu- ally, the ability to disrupt cell structures. DESs are solvents that can be chemically tailored due to their ability to be synthesized by combining various quaternary ammonium salts with several HBDs. Different cations and anions can be used to make different DESs, allowing for greater control over their water compatibility. They are denser than water, miscible with high-polarity substances, and can dissolve inorganic and organic constituents. DESs have many advantageous properties in chemistry and physics, including moderate viscosity, low freezing point, density, conductivity, and high thermal stability. The main physicochemical properties of DESs will be described and discussed in this section. 7.1. _Melting point (MP)_ DESs, as previously stated, have a lower melting point than any of their compounds. Conclusion Adsorption is essential in analytical procedures, mainly when the environmental sample analysis or sample matrices are complex. Analytical performance is significantly impacted by selecting the best adsorbent solvent. The DESs have a broad spectrum of applications in the separation sciences, not just for their "greenness" but also for their extraordinary physicochemical properties. The DESs-based adsorbent has excellent molecular recognition efficiency in the aqueous phase. It is prepared in the aqueous media, escaping the consumption of a large quantity of traditional organic solvents. Due to its outstanding property, it simultaneously plays a porogen and imprinting path for the targeted analyte. Because of its ionizable nature, in the DESs the stronger hydrogen bonding, offers unique behaviour from the traditional solvents when used in the extraction process. However, the DESs-based adsorbents applications are still deficient, and the advantages of DESs over the outdated solvents have not been fully revealed. So that more efforts should be made to examine better DESs species for chromatographic separation techniques. It will be stimulating to explore the DESs adsorbents-based new environmental applications. ## 10. Future aspects The DESs-based adsorbent materials need more attention and research to explore the new modifications and applications in the separation sciences. DESs-based adsorbent materials have been used successfully to extract and separate a wide range of analytes like aromatic hydrocarbons, biodiesel, gases, metal, and metal. Still, researchers focused on modifying mobile and stationary phases for chromatographic techniques such as GC and HPLC; additionally, DESs should be used for the sample preparation for chromatographic determination. So it can be predicted that the use of DESs should be enhanced to advance new robust and chromatographic methods. In this prospect, it must be explored the temperature effect and the effect of water quantity on the DESs preparation and stability. It is important to emphasize different applied fields such as electrochemistry, separation sciences, pharmaceuticals and drug delivery if we expect that DESs will be used in analytical chemistry in ways other than as extractants. The use of DESs in this field has enormous potential that is essentially unexplored. Only a little bit of work has been completed in this area. Additionally, more research needs to be done on how DESs affect chromatography separation, including the potential use of DESs as a stationary phase in gas chromatography, a capillary modifier, or a mobile phase in electrophoresis as substitutes for ionic liquids. A wide range of work is also made possible by synthesizing and modifying adsor-bents in DESs media for additional applications in analytical chemistry. The scope of study in this field virtually expands to in-finity when we consider that it is possible to combine several areas, such as the fabrication of MIPs on the surface of electrodes in a DES medium. Therefore, we suggest that analytical chemistry re-searchers concentrate on using the potential application of DESs in the separation sciences and employing them in various areas. In actuality, DESs have not yet been used in conjunction with such directions as microfluidic analysis, the creation of paper micro-chips, luminescence and chemiluminescence, surface plasmon resonance, electrophoresis, sampling, and sample preparation. In the future, combining nanotechnology with DESs needs deep exploration and applications in separation sciences. Combining nanotechnology and DESs will open new doors in the separation sciences.
